title: The Opera Game
black: Duke Karl of Brunswick and Count Isouard (consulting)
source: Public-domain game score, Paris 1858. Notes written for Trivium Chess.
intro:
Paul Morphy played this game in Paris in 1858 against two amateurs who were consulting each other on their moves. It is short, it is famous, and nearly every move connects to the ideas in this unit: loose pieces, counting, and what happens when one side develops and the other doesn't.

You will play Morphy's side. The first moves are shown. From move 7 you guess each of Morphy's moves before seeing it. A different move isn't necessarily wrong, so treat the comparison as a conversation, not a grade.

prompts.12: The knight on f6 has blocked your queen's line to f7. Find a queen move that attacks something loose and keeps an eye on f7.
prompts.14: Black has defended f7. You could take on b7. Is there something more useful to do?
prompts.16: Black's knight on f6 stands in front of the queen on e7. How can you use that?
prompts.18: Black's pawn attacks your bishop on c4. Retreating is safe. Look for something sharper.
prompts.20: Keep the pressure on. Black's king is still in the centre.
prompts.22: Which White piece hasn't joined the game yet?
prompts.24: The knight on d7 is pinned. Count what attacks it and what defends it.
prompts.30: Find the finish. It begins with the most surprising move on the board.

notes.5: Black pins the knight on f3 to the queen behind it. If the knight moves, the queen on d1 is exposed.
notes.7: Black gives up the bishop for the knight rather than lose the e5 pawn.
notes.8: The queen recaptures and is already developed, looking down the f-file at f7.
notes.10: Count on f7 now: the queen and the bishop attack it, and only the king defends it.
notes.11: Black defends by blocking: the knight on f6 cuts the queen off from f7.
notes.12: One move, two jobs. The queen attacks the loose pawn on b7, and it stands behind the bishop, ready to support it on f7.
notes.13: The queen on e7 covers f7. The pawn on b7 is still hanging.
notes.14: Morphy leaves b7 alone. After Qxb7, Black has ...Qb4+ and the queens come off. With the queens on, Morphy's lead in development counts for much more.
notes.15: Now the Black queen protects b7 along the seventh rank.
notes.16: A pin with teeth: the knight on f6 can't move without exposing the queen on e7.
notes.17: Black tries to push the bishop away and gain space.
notes.18: Morphy gives a knight to rip open lines. The Black king is still in the centre, and most Black pieces are still at home.
notes.20: Check, and the knight on b8 has to block. Black's pieces are getting in each other's way.
notes.22: Castling brings the rook straight to the d-file, where it attacks the pinned knight on d7.
notes.23: Black adds a defender to d7.
notes.24: Morphy gives the exchange, rook for knight, to keep the attack going. Every move now is forcing.
notes.26: The last White piece arrives. Count on d7 again: two attackers, two defenders, but one of the defenders is the pinned knight.
notes.28: The bishop takes on d7 with check, pulling the f6 knight away from where it was.
notes.29: Black has to recapture. The knight is now the only thing guarding d8.
notes.30: The queen offers itself. The knight on d7 is overworked: it cannot both take on b8 and keep guarding d8.
notes.32: Checkmate. The rook gives check, and the bishop on g5 covers e7 and d8. Every White piece that moved played a part.

outro: Morphy used every piece. Black moved the queen, both knights, and the pawns, but the bishop on f8 and the rook on h8 never played a role. Count the moves each side spent getting pieces into play, and you have most of the explanation.
